author_observation: Functional styles are systematic language realizations conditioned by domains of activity and communicative/social factors.
boundary: Do not infer style from one lexical or syntactic feature.

author_observation: Style is modeled through selection and organization/combination of linguistic means into a communicative whole.
boundary: Individual forms are not stylistic rules outside text-level organization.

author_observation: Standard-language and stylistic norms differ in character and degree of obligatoriness.
boundary: Stylistic preference must never be promoted into hard NORM without independent evidence.

author_observation: The book distinguishes literary-artistic, publicistic, scientific, administrative and conversational functional styles.
boundary: Profiles are abstractions; real texts can be mixed and genre-specific.

author_observation: Functional-style hierarchy includes complexes, interstyles, substyles and genres, with border zones between major styles.
boundary: Do not force one document-level label when sections serve different functions.

author_observation: Switching between functional codes can be productive when the target code's logic is understood and appropriate.
boundary: Style mixing is not an error by itself.

author_observation: Style and decoding depend on sender, receiver, channel, code, prior knowledge and communicative noise.
boundary: Readability and naturalness are audience-relative.

author_observation: Economy reduces transmission cost while redundancy increases reliability; functional styles balance them differently.
boundary: Neither shorter nor less repetitive is universally better.

author_observation: Standardization, unification and recurring formulas can improve decoding speed, accuracy and reliability in administrative and publicistic communication.
boundary: Template regularity can still become excessive; function and genre determine the boundary.

author_observation: Publicistic style targets broad audiences and combines informing with influence/persuasion to varying degrees by genre.
boundary: Persuasive or emotional language is not automatically inappropriate in publicistic genres.

author_observation: Publicistic style is genre-diverse, media-dependent and porous toward other styles/codes.
boundary: Journalistic/public text can legitimately contain conversational, scientific or literary elements.

author_observation: Scientific style favors logical, abstract, objective, precise and terminological expression with restricted expressive-emotional material.
boundary: Science popularization and pedagogical genres may be more personal or expressive.

author_observation: Strict scientific prose often uses complex multi-clause syntax to represent complex reasoning and precision relations.
boundary: Complexity is not a license for unreadable syntax; sentence length alone is not diagnostic.

author_observation: Standardization and unification are central constitutive mechanisms of administrative style and document production.
boundary: Standardization serves institutional processing but does not excuse unnecessary opacity.

author_observation: Administrative style contains distinct agreement/contract, directive, legislative-legal, personal-document and correspondence realizations.
boundary: Do not flatten legal, business and correspondence registers into one bureaucratic profile.

author_observation: Conversational style is narrower than oral speech; scientific discussion, broadcast speech and street conversation can all be oral but belong to different functional styles.
boundary: Channel (spoken/written) does not determine register.

author_observation: Conversational style often uses simple syntax, ellipsis, pauses, fragments and repeated/frozen constructions.
boundary: Written imitation of conversation and actual chat differ; preserve only when context supports conversational function.

author_observation: Intonation and non-verbal cues help organize topic/focus and meaning in conversational interaction.
boundary: Text-only systems cannot confidently reconstruct missing prosody.

author_observation: Literary-artistic style permits foregrounding, rhythm, figures, repetition and marked organization for aesthetic effect.
boundary: Creative markedness must not be normalized just because it is rare in expository prose.

author_observation: Formal/stylistic choices carry information about sender, receiver, code and communicative process beyond propositional content.
boundary: A semantic-preserving rewrite can still be stylistically lossy.

author_observation: Recurring templates and clichés can be functional in high-standardization genres and need not be stylistic errors.
boundary: Do not suppress existing structural signals globally; instead require genre-aware interpretation.

author_observation: Informational publicistic genres tend toward logical succession and compact factual structures, while literary-publicistic genres allow parcellation and expressive sentence forms.
boundary: No single journalistic sentence template is universal.

author_observation: The source reflects a 2002 South-Slavic/post-Yugoslav scholarly environment and uses cross-language evidence.
boundary: Exact lexical, grammatical and normative claims require current Serbian verification.

author_observation: The stylistic value of a linguistic feature depends on the functional system, genre and communicative purpose in which it occurs.
boundary: A feature may be natural in one register and awkward in another.
